It was Pongal week in the village, and the school had a kolam contest. Vikas stood next to his friend Chandrika, looking at the entries.

"Bittu's is ugly," he said.

Chandrika frowned. "It's the best one. Look at the peacock."

"He cheated in the maths test last month. I saw him."

"What does that have to do with the kolam?"

"He's just bad. Everything about him."

Just then, Bittu came over with a plate of sweet pongal and offered it to both of them. Vikas didn't take any. "He's only being nice to show off."

Chandrika took a piece. "Vikas, he copied once. That was wrong. But he can still draw a good peacock."

The peacock really was beautiful. He took a small piece of pongal, slowly.

qa.q: What was in Bittu's kolam?
qa.a: Look at the peacock.

qa.q: Why did Vikas think everything about Bittu was bad?
qa.a: Vikas felt angry and distrustful after seeing Bittu cheat, so that one wrong act made his drawing and kindness seem bad too.

qa.q: What did Chandrika say that helped Vikas look again?
qa.a: Chandrika pointed out that copying once was wrong but didn't make Bittu's peacock less beautiful, separating the one flaw from the rest.

qa.q: How might Bittu feel when Vikas refused the pongal?
qa.a: Bittu might feel hurt and confused, since he was trying to be friendly.

grounding: During a harvest festival, a child who saw a classmate cheat decides his drawing and kindness are bad too.

It was Ramadan in Amman, and after iftar the children played board games in Sami's building. Last week, Sami had seen Omar move his counter an extra square when he thought nobody was looking.

Now Sami didn't trust anything Omar did. When Omar laughed, it sounded fake.

Tonight Omar brought a big box of dates for everyone. Sami refused. "He's just trying to look good."

His older sister said, "Sami, he cheated in a game. That doesn't mean everything he does is bad."

"But he's a cheater."

"He was a cheater once, in one game. Look, he's sharing with everyone."

Sami watched Omar give the last date to the youngest boy. He felt a little uncertain for the first time.

qa.a: A big box of dates for everyone.

qa.q: How might Omar feel when Sami refused the dates?

During winter sports week, Suraj's class had a quiz. Suraj saw Ronak glance at his neighbour's paper. From then on, Suraj decided Ronak was bad.

When Ronak scored a goal in the football match, Suraj said, "He probably fouled someone." When Ronak helped a Class 2 child tie his shoelaces, Suraj muttered, "Showing off."

Aadhya, sitting on the bench, heard him. "Suraj, you're being unfair."

"He cheats!"

"He looked at a paper once. Was his goal a cheat?"

Suraj thought. The goal was clean. Everyone saw it.

"And the shoelaces?"

Suraj didn't answer. He had been so sure that one bad thing meant everything was bad. Now he wasn't sure at all.

passage:
Class teacher's note, Class 9B

When I took over 9B this term, the previous teacher's handover note said: "Shankar: lazy. Doesn't try." I noticed the other teachers say the same thing about him in the staff room.

But in my first month, Shankar has submitted every science assignment on time. His diagram of the water cycle was the best in the class. When I mentioned it in the staff room, one teacher said, "He must have copied it."

When Shankar forgets his notebook, it's reported. When he answers well, nobody mentions it. I think the label has stuck so hard that people only see what fits it.

Today I asked Shankar how he feels in class. He shrugged and said, "Everyone thinks I'm lazy, so why try?"

I've shared his last month's work with the other teachers and asked them to notice his effort for two weeks.

Sarika

qa.q: What did the previous teacher's handover note say about Shankar?
qa.a: Shankar: lazy. Doesn't try.

qa.q: How does Shankar feel about the label?
qa.a: Shankar feels discouraged and hopeless, saying everyone thinks he's lazy so there is no point trying.

qa.q: What did Sarika do to help break the label?
qa.a: Sarika shared Shankar's actual work with other teachers and asked them to notice his effort for two weeks.

qa.q: How might the other teachers see Shankar after two weeks of noticing?
qa.a: They may start seeing his effort and good work that the label had hidden.

grounding: A teacher notes a teenager labelled lazy whose good work is ignored while every slip is noticed.

The group project was due in three days, and the hostel internet had been down since morning. Noor was stressed.

Tenzin had been late with his part last week, by a whole day. Since then, Noor hadn't given him anything new to do. "He's useless," she told the others. "I'll do his section myself."

Tonight, Noor was trying to write the data analysis. She was stuck. The formulas weren't working.

Tenzin knocked on her door with a printed sheet. "I did the analysis offline yesterday. On my laptop. Thought it might help."

Noor stared at it. The formulas were clean. The charts were better than hers.

"You were late once," she said slowly, "and I decided you couldn't do anything."

Tenzin shrugged. "My grandfather was sick that week. I should have told you."

Noor felt her face go hot. She handed him the next section to do.

qa.a: Noor felt embarrassed and a bit ashamed, realising she had judged him useless from one late submission.

qa.a: Noor could ask what happened before deciding, and keep giving tasks based on the teammate's whole record.

qa.a: Tenzin may have felt left out and unfairly judged, especially since he was dealing with a family problem.

From then on, she gave all the important tasks to the other two. Naveen got to format fonts.

When Naveen suggested an idea in the meeting, Rekha barely listened. When he sent a message, she didn't reply. In her mind, he was the late one, and that was all.

Rekha almost said no. Then she thought about it. She had never actually seen his skills. She'd only seen one late day.

He sent the analysis by midnight. It was excellent.

Rekha sent him a message: "I'm sorry. I judged you by one mistake."

On Monday morning a wrong shipment went to their biggest client in Surat, and it was Anirban's mistake. Nazia, the team lead, felt a wave of anger. She began drafting a note to HR: "Repeated carelessness."

Then she stopped at the word "repeated".

Was it? She realised she was angry about this one error, and that anger was painting everything. She pulled up Anirban's record for the past year. Eighty-two shipments. One error before this, eight months ago. Three thank-you notes from clients.

She also checked what had happened on Monday. The warehouse system had shown the wrong code for two hours because of an update. Two other teams had made the same mistake.

Nazia deleted the draft. She called Anirban in and said, "This was a costly error. Walk me through what happened." She listened. Then she asked IT to look at the system update.

qa.q: How many shipments had Anirban handled in the past year?
qa.a: Eighty-two shipments.

qa.a: Nazia felt a wave of anger about the error, which was colouring her view of Anirban's work.

qa.q: What did Nazia do before deciding, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Nazia reviewed Anirban's full record and the context of the system update, which showed one error shouldn't define him.

qa.q: How might Anirban feel being asked to walk through what happened?
qa.a: Anirban may feel nervous but respected, since he's asked to explain rather than being blamed straight away.

grounding: A lead notices anger over one error is colouring her view and reviews the person's full record and context before deciding.

Zainab, one of my best agents, sent a rude-sounding reply to a customer. The customer complained to my boss. I was embarrassed and angry. By evening, I'd started thinking: maybe Zainab's attitude has always been a bit off.

So I looked properly. Her satisfaction scores for the year were the highest on the team. She'd handled two of our hardest escalations. And that day, she'd been covering three people's queues because of a sick day.

I talked to her the next morning. She was mortified about the reply. She'd typed it fast between two angry calls.

We agreed she'd take a proper break when queues pile up, and I'd spread the load. One slip, not a pattern.

I'm Damini. Last term, I was so angry with Arohi.

She didn't come to my birthday. She didn't reply to my messages for four days. When she came back to school, she was quiet and didn't even say sorry. I told everyone she was selfish. I thought, that's just who she is.

A week later, our class teacher mentioned that Arohi's family had been moving house suddenly. Her father's job had changed cities. They'd packed in three days. She'd been sleeping on boxes.

I felt awful. I had decided she was selfish without even wondering if something was wrong.

I went to find her at lunch. I said sorry. She said, "I wanted to tell you, but everything was so messy."

Now when someone goes quiet, I try to remember Arohi's boxes. There's usually a reason I can't see.

Week one. Zeenat was assigned to a lab group with Tushar. He arrived late to the first session, yawning. She thought, great, a lazy one.

Week three. Tushar missed a deadline for his part of the report. Zeenat complained to the others. "He's just careless. I'm doing his part." She didn't ask him why.

Week five. Zeenat went to the canteen early, before seven, and saw Tushar coming out of the kitchen in an apron, carrying crates. The canteen manager said, "He's been working the night-to-morning shift here since his mother lost her job."

Zeenat felt her stomach drop. She'd been sure it was his character. It had never crossed her mind that something invisible was pressing on him.

That afternoon she found him in the library. "I'm sorry. I didn't know. Can we split the report differently so it works with your shifts?"

He looked relieved. "Thank you. I didn't know how to say it."

Anand, you said your roommate is lazy because he sleeps all afternoon? Hmm. Sit. Your Indu aunty has a story.

When I was nineteen, at college in Madurai, our group had a boy called Selvam. He always came late to morning lectures. He fell asleep in the library. I said to everyone, "Selvam is lazy. Don't give him anything important."

One night, going home late from a wedding, I passed the bus depot. There was Selvam, washing buses under a street light. At one in the morning.

I found out later he washed buses every night to pay his hostel fees. His family were farmers, and it had been a bad year.

I felt so ashamed. I'd judged him by the sleepy face I saw, never thinking about the nights I didn't see.

So, Anand, have you asked your roommate what his nights are like?

At the small design agency in Berlin, Tuan had sent the client the wrong file version twice in one week. The account manager was ready to report him. "He's careless."

Selin, who sat next to Tuan, paused. She'd worked with him for a year. He'd never done this before.

"Before we decide, can I talk to him?"

She found him in the kitchen, making a very strong coffee. "Tuan, is everything okay? The file mix-ups aren't like you."

He sighed. "My father's in hospital in Hanoi. I've been on video calls at four in the morning. I'm exhausted. I'm sorry."

Selin nodded. "That would make anyone slip. But let's also fix the file naming. It's been messy for months."

She went back to the account manager. "There's something hard happening for him, and our file system has a gap too. Both are true."

qa.a: Selin asked Tuan what was happening before deciding, then recognised both his situation and a real gap in the file naming system.

qa.a: Tuan probably felt relieved and supported, able to share what was going on.

In the admin office of a Pune hospital, Abhinav had misfiled three patient billing forms in one week. The supervisor sighed. "He's getting sloppy."

Anand, who shared a desk with Abhinav, didn't agree straight away. He'd seen Abhinav stay late to fix other people's errors.

At lunch, Anand asked, "Hey, this week seems rough. Is something going on?"

Abhinav rubbed his eyes. "The new filing system changed on Monday. Nobody trained me. I've been guessing."

Anand checked. It was true: the system had been updated, and only the morning shift had been trained.

But Anand also noticed Abhinav's desk was stacked with unsorted papers from weeks before the change.

He told the supervisor, "He wasn't trained on the new system. That needs fixing. And his desk backlog was building up before that. Maybe we help him with both."

Dear Zubin,

I wanted to write rather than say this in the meeting.

Over the last two weeks, three of your reports have come in with missing sections. The team lead mentioned it, and I could see people starting to think you'd become careless.

I don't want to jump to that. You've been one of the most careful people on this team for two years. So I'm asking: is something going on? A heavier workload, something at home, the new software? Anything I can help with?

I also want to be honest: I've noticed you've stopped using the checklist we made last year. That might be part of it too.

Both can be true, a hard patch and a habit slipping. If it's either, let's sort it out together. If it's both, even better that we talk now.

Let's have tea tomorrow?

Sharmila

It was Makar Sankranti, and after the kites the village boys played cricket in the harvested field. Saurabh's team won the first match. "Because I'm the best batsman," he announced, puffing out his chest.

In the second match, he was out for zero. He threw down the bat. "This bat is cracked! And the bowler was throwing, not bowling!"

His sister Rajni, keeping score on a mud wall, called out, "It's the same bat you won with!"

"It cracked in between."

"And the same bowler?"

"He got better at cheating."

Rajni laughed. "So when you win, it's you. When you lose, it's the bat, the bowler and the field."

Saurabh scowled. But he picked up the bat and looked at it. There was no crack.

It was Chinese New Year in Singapore, and the cousins were playing badminton in the void deck. Wei beat Liam in the first game. "I'm just really good," he said.

In the second game, Liam won easily. Wei stamped his foot. "The wind was blowing my way. And my racket strings are loose."

"The wind was blowing both ways," said Liam. "And you used the same racket when you won."

"It got loose after."

"You always do this," Liam said. "When you win, you're good. When you lose, it's the wind."

Wei's grandmother said, "Wei, maybe both games were you. The good one and the bad one."

Wei frowned. He hadn't thought about it that way. If the losing was his too, then maybe he could get better.

"Maybe I made a mistake," he mumbled.
